The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Actualitate » Today in the News » Moldova’s new Prime Minister on a visit to Bucharest Moldova’s new Prime Minister on a visit to Bucharest The Prime Minister of the Republic of Moldova, Vasile Tofan, met in Bucharest with the Romanian Head of State, Nicușor Dan, and his counterpart, Ilie Bolojan Premierul Republicii Moldova, Vasile Tofan şi preşedintele României, Nicuşor Dan Leyla Cheamil , 31.07.2026, 14:00 Vasile Tofan, Prime Minister of the Republic of Moldova – a former Soviet state with a predominantly Romanian-speaking population – Thursday made his first foreign visit to Romania since taking office. He was received by the Head of State, Nicuşor Dan, who reaffirmed Romania’s firm and consistent support for the country’s integration into the European Union. The President also welcomed the opening of the first rounds of negotiations on Moldova’s accession to the EU. “We have reaffirmed the privileged nature of the relationship between Romania and the Republic of Moldova and our commitment to continuing the development of joint projects, particularly in the economic, energy and transport sectors. These projects contribute to strengthening the resilience and prosperity of both countries and the entire region,’ Nicușor Dan added. The two officials welcomed the recent signing of the agreement for the construction of the new bridge at Ungheni, which will form part of the future link to the A8 motorway, as well as the contract for work on Section 4 of the latter. Furthermore, Nicușor Dan emphasised the support that Bucharest was providing to Chișinău with regard to strengthening resilience and security. In this context, a key focus of the discussions was the complex security situation in the region, caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and its consequences for neighbouring states. Prime Minister Vasile Tofan expressed his gratitude for the constant and unconditional support provided by Romania. “I must say from the outset that I am coming home, I am Romanian, and I fully intend to contribute to strengthening this strategic – but, first and foremost, fraternal – relationship between our countries,” the official from Chișinău added. He was also received by the acting Romanian Prime Minister, Ilie Bolojan, who, for his part, stated that Romania would remain Chișinău’s main supporter in the process of accession to the European Union, offering the experience it had gained as a Member State and its political and diplomatic support. During the meeting, the two officials reviewed the progress of joint projects and ways of accelerating them, with a focus on those in the transport and energy sectors, which are intended to help ensure better interconnection between the two banks of the Prut. They discussed the construction of two new 400-kilovolt interconnection lines, Suceava–Bălți and Gutinaș–Strășeni, and, in the field of infrastructure, port and rail interconnection projects. The Moldovan official stated that he did not want economic relations to be limited solely to trade and exports. “We want more Romanian investment in the Republic of Moldova, companies that produce together, shared value chains, and industrial, technological and energy projects,” Vasile Tofan emphasised. The President of the Senate, Mircea Abrudean, stated after his meeting with the Prime Minister of the Republic of Moldova that the two countries enjoy a solid and consistent partnership, particularly in key areas of development for both nations – energy, infrastructure and digitalisation. Vasile Tofan also met with the Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Sorin Grindeanu, with whom he discussed the harmonisation of the Republic of Moldova’s legislation with European Union regulations. For weeks Berlin was flooded with portraits of her wearing a nameplate necklace with the word Mietendeckel (rent freeze).’ Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters Opinion Germany Berlin’s new political star is offering something all of Europe needs – hope and housing Fatma Aydemir Elif Eralp wants lower rents and more public housing. It’s not rocket science but mainstream parties still don’t get why they are failing Fri 25 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 00.02 EDT Share H ope is a fragile thing. You can only hold on to it as long as you find reasons to believe tomorrow can be better. A woman, for instance, who has the resources and opportunity to rent her own flat will be more likely to leave her abusive husband and recover. A pupil who has their own room and desk to do their homework might find more meaning in thriving at school. And an elderly person who can afford to live in a neighbourhood where they feel safe and connected is less likely to become isolated and depressed. It’s not by chance that the examples above all revolve around the same topic. Affordable housing is possibly the most personal and most urgent social issue of our time. In Berlin, a city where 85% of residents live in rented accommodation, rents have risen by almost 70% in the past 10 years. And that is despite a rent control law that has been in effect since 2015. How? Loopholes and illegal practices have allowed property owners to continue putting pressure on the housing market. The social anxiety caused by this crisis, far from affecting just low-earners and single-parent households, affects vast parts of the middle class, too. So what does a political party need to do to get into power in the state of Berlin? It’s really not rocket science: focus on the housing crisis, provide solutions and avoid distractions by political opponents. This is exactly what the leftwing party Die Linke has been doing for months. The result of last Sunday’s state election is striking: for the first time, Die Linke, with 25.7%, became the strongest party in Berlin. Not because everyone who voted for it suddenly agreed with everything else the party stands for. But because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price. The result is also remarkable because Germany is at a historic turning point: on the same day as the Berlin election, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged – with 38% – as the largest party in a state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania . Just two weeks previously, it had secured a victory in Saxony-Anhalt with almost 44%. While the centrist parties, in an attempt to win back their voters, are desperately mimicking the AfD’s ideas and rhetoric on migration, Die Linke could set an example in Berlin for the rest of the country: by actually listening to people’s worries and working on ideas to improve their lives sustainably, instead of scapegoating. The party’s lead candidate, Elif Eralp, could become not only Berlin’s first mayor from the left since Germany’s reunification in 1990, but also Berlin’s first mayor ever with a migration background. Born in Munich, she is the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled following the military coup in Turkey in 1980. Eralp put housing at the centre of her campaign. For many weeks the whole city was flooded with giant portraits of the 45-year-old wearing an optimistic smile and a golden nameplate necklace with the word Mietendeckel (rent freeze). Eralp’s programme was clear from the start: lower rents, more public housing and the implementation of Berlin’s 2021 referendum in which a majority voted for more public ownership of housing to alleviate the accommodation crisis. It’s not a completely new world that Eralp promises. All she had to do was simply speak about the one we are already living in. But winning an election is one thing. Governing is another. Die Linke may have won the most seats, but it lacks a majority to run the state on its own. To turn its campaign promises into policy, Eralp has to negotiate with other parties, particularly the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. While Berlin’s Greens have already spoken out in favour of a progressive coalition, the SPD is deeply divided . Die Linke’s top priority is a radical ambition : it would involve the compulsory purchase of the housing portfolios (which exceed 3,000 apartments) of large private real estate companies and their transfer into a democratically controlled non-profit, public body. The SPD’s approach is to regulate the housing market much more strongly, expand public housing and potentially introduce a rent cap. Which sounds like everything that has already failed in the last decade. At the same time, Die Linke enters negotiations under a microscope. Political opponents are questioning whether the party’s positions are compatible with democratic values, while controversies surrounding antisemitism and parts of the party’s political culture have become a major subject of public debate. Antisemitism is, historically and today, a problem inherent in German society as a whole, one that also exists within Die Linke and should be combated more decisively. However, the uproar about antisemitic rappers and an organised crime member who was spotted at Die Linke’s election party seem like sham debates that overshadow the actual conflicts of interest. Meanwhile, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has already stated, in response to the Berlin elections, that a federal law could be passed to prevent the expropriation of privately owned housing. Markus Söder, leader of the state of Bavaria, announced financial consequences for Berlin, if the “extremist”, “antidemocratic” and “antisemitic” Die Linke were to govern the capital. No such measures were announced for potential AfD-governed states, of course. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion It is hardly surprising that conservatives are now foaming at the mouth, given that for decades they have been pursuing policies that benefit those who profit from the housing crisis. Yet, more and more Social Democrats are also up in arms , putting pressure on their party not to form a coalition with Die Linke. And this is where hope becomes fragile again. Because Eralp now has to do something harder than naming a problem: she has to find coalition partners, and for that she has to compromise – without making her voters feel betrayed. Now that would be a radical act, indeed.
